Beállítom Halálos tömegszerencsétlenség gondatlan okozása miatt indított eljárást a rendőrség a vasárnap az M3-as autópályán történt balesetet szenvedett busz vezetője ellen – közölte a Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság sajtóreferense hétfőn az MTI-vel. Varga Rudolf azt mondta, a sofőrt őrizetbe vették , letartóztatásáról a napokban dönthet a bíróság. A lengyel zarándokokat szállító busz vasárnap hajnalban borult fel az M3-as autópályán Mezőkeresztesnél. Tizenkét ember meghalt , és többen súlyosan megsérültek. A rendőrség elsődleges adatai szerint a sofőr feltehetően elaludt. A medjugorjei zarándokútról érkező buszon 57 utas és a két sofőr utazott, mindannyian lengyel állampolgárok. A Miskolcra szállított kilenc sérült közül kettőt súlyos, életveszélyes, de jelenleg stabil állapotban kezelnek a Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén Vármegyei Központi Kórház és Egyetemi Oktatókórház Központi Aneszteziológiai és Intenzív Terápiás Osztályán. Németh Csaba, a kórház sajtóreferense hétfőn azt mondta, hogy mindkét súlyos sérültnél műtéti beavatkozásra van szükség, az egyik beteg a közlés időpontjában is a műtőben volt. A miskolci kórház traumatológiai osztályán öt beteget kezelnek, ellátásuk a sérüléseik jellegének és súlyosságának megfelelően történik. Egy sérült vasárnap ambuláns ellátást követően távozott a kórházból, egy gerincsérültet pedig az idegsebészeti osztályon tartanak megfigyelés alatt. Ő – további kórházi kezelésre – szállítható állapotban van. Az időközben érkezett tizenhét hozzátartozó számára lengyel tolmácsot biztosítanak. A hozzátartozók a kórházban fekvő családtagokkal folyamatosan tartják a kapcsolatot, az orvosoktól felvilágosítást kaptak a kezelt hozzátartozójuk állapotáról, és szállást is biztosítottak nekik Miskolcon. Az egri Markhot Ferenc Kórházban is megkezdték a sérültek hazaszállításának szervezését – közölte hétfőn az intézmény sajtóreferense. Szegedi Erzsébet az MTI-nek azt mondta, a buszbaleset tíz sérültjét ápolják náluk, hetet a traumatológiai, kettőt az ortopédiai, egyet pedig az intenzív osztályon. Mindegyikük állapota stabil, nem életveszélyes, többen még további vizsgálatokra várnak. Négy sérült állapota súlyos, ők jellemzően nyakcsigolya-, hátcsigolya-, illetve koponyatörést szenvedtek. A kórházba megérkeztek a lengyel nagykövetség és konzulátus munkatársai, akik egyeztetik és szervezik a sérültek hazaszállítását. Munkájukat két tolmács segíti. Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock Jamie Oliver Jamie and Jools Oliver pay themselves £1.7m dividend as profits almost halve Pre-tax earnings slump at chef’s food and media group after one-off costs including for a new cookery school Sarah Butler Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jamie and Jools Oliver have paid themselves a £1.7m dividend – more than 40% down on last year – after profits at their cookery and media empire almost halved. Sales at Jamie Oliver Holdings remained broadly steady at £28.4m in 2025, £160,000 less than in the previous year, as a strong performance at the group’s own restaurants, franchise business, cookery schools and TV productions offset a decline in royalties, licensing and endorsements. “We have delivered new Jamie Oliver titles in both book and TV formats during the year and there has been a continued strong performance from back catalogue book titles and our international television content distribution,” accounts filed at Companies House said. The Eat Yourself Healthy cookbook was a No 1 global bestseller, selling nearly 70,000 copies in its first week, making it one of Jamie’s fastest-selling books. However, pre-tax profits at the group, which became a certified B Corp in 2019 , slumped to £1.25m, from £2.4m a year before, after £1.46m of exceptional costs related to a business restructure in which about 20 jobs were lost from the Olivers’ media team. Profits were also affected by pre-opening costs on a new cookery school in John Lewis’s Oxford Street outlet in London. Sales at owned and operated restaurants rose 17% to £4.3m and sales via the mainly overseas franchise restaurants, such as Jamie Oliver’s Deli and Jamie Oliver Kitchen, rose 6.5% to £4m. Cookery school income soared 48% to £1.6m. The group opened Jamie Oliver Catherine Street, his return to the UK restaurant scene with a menu focused on British produce, in 2023. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion ‘We don’t want to make the same mistakes’: Jamie’s Italian reopens in London Read more Last December, Oliver also opened a new Jamie’s Italian in London’s Leicester Square, backed by the Prezzo owner Brava Hospitality Group, seven years after the chain collapsed. The original chain called in administrators in 2019, leaving £83m of debt and causing 1,000 job losses. Brava’s backers have suggested there could be scope for up to 40 more of the new restaurants in the UK, and one more is planned this year if the right site can be secured. A spokesperson for Oliver said 10 new franchise restaurants under his name were planned to open this year around the world, including one just opened in Abu Dhabi after openings in Bahrain and India. However, royalties, licensing and endorsement income – which is by far the biggest part of the Oliver business and includes a Tefal pan range – slid by close to £2m to £15.9m. It was the second year of sliding income from this angle for Oliver, after a major deal with Tesco in 2023 ended in 2024. L on Hancock’s Santa Maria campus, 800 S. College Drive. Gallery hours are 9 a.m.-5 p.m. Monday-Friday. Admission is free. Sign Up for the A.M. The display brings together works primarily from Pazderka’s “Nostalgie” and “Family Album” series, which explore memory, identity, loss, natural disaster, and the fleeting nature of human existence. There will be an artist talk and reception 4-7 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 2. Pazderka is known for creating paintings using unconventional materials including ash, charcoal, oil paint, and charred wood. He began incorporating ash into his work after witnessing devastating wildfires in Santa Barbara County, using the material to explore the tension between destruction and beauty. “My interest has always been how to make something that is not only materially interesting but conceptually engaging,” Pazderka said. “The goal is to make something visually compelling that also creates a doorway into difficult subject matter.” His “Nostalgie” series depicts towering wildfire clouds that appear both beautiful and threatening, inviting viewers to consider humanity’s relationship with powerful natural forces, organizers said. Rather than simply documenting destruction, Pazderka uses the imagery to explore ideas of impermanence, catastrophe and mortality. The “Family Album” series takes a more personal approach. Created from old family photographs, the paintings reflect Pazderka’s experience as an immigrant and his evolving relationship with memory, family and identity. He began the series after his mother returned to the Czech Republic following nearly three decades in the United States. So much of what’s in a family album is unknown and unknowable,” Pazderka said. “The paintings become a way of remembering, but also a way of exploring those images for myself and imagining those places as somehow becoming part of me.” Pazderka has been making art for decades and has exhibited internationally. His work often combines personal history with broader philosophical questions about how people understand their place in the world and how memory changes over time. For more, contact gallery co-director Elizabeth Russell at erussell@hancockcollege.edu or visit www.hancockcollege.edu/gallery . https://www.bikeradar.com/features/opini.text: ROAD MTB GRAVEL ELECTRIC WOMEN BEGINNERS MAGAZINE OFFERS YOUTUBE Best Products Reviews News Features Advice Travel Magazines Podcast Rondo’s return from bankruptcy is a boon for bicycle design – other brands should take note of the Polish innovator The Polish bike maker's resurgence should encourage others to embrace bold design Rondo Warren Rossiter Last month's news that Polish innovator Rondo is set to return under new ownership, but with the same design team, brought a smile to my face. That's not just because I was a fan of Rondo’s designs, but because the brand's demise in 2024 seemed to signal that being different was too risky in the current bike-business climate. Over the last decade, the prevalence of wind-tunnel testing, CFD software and tube-profile libraries has meant a lot of bike design has become predictable. Or perhaps some of the biggest brands have been playing things too ‘safe’. Just look at the latest Trek Domane . It has lost its revolutionary vibration-damping IsoSpeed technology and now it’s just another lightweight endurance bike . Although I’m sure it’ll be a great bike and I’m looking forward to trying it out, I think that’s a shame and I miss the bold confidence of the earlier designs. A beautiful example of a curly stayed Harry Hetchins. Rob Spedding Perhaps it has always been this way. Bike design on the whole stays ‘safe’. In the golden age of steel-only, lug shapes and paint made road bikes distinctive (bar a few outliers such as Hetchins with its curly stays). However, the bikes that stay in my memory are the ones that break the mould in pursuit of something innovative or new, be it performance or aesthetics. Read more: Rondo is back from bankruptcy – and the innovative brand's original design team is coming with it Made to stand out Cannondale's Raven: monocoque, Lefty fork, innovative and bold. I remember the first time I saw the Cannondale Raven in 2000 with a single-sided Lefty fork. It was a unique design that continues to this day and is found on the brilliant Topstone gravel bike. The Raven looked radical enough with its monocoque frame, but combined with the Lefty fork, it stood out like a beacon the first time I saw one on the shop floor at Bristol’s Mud Dock Cycles. Before that, Giant’s TCR reshaped the humble road bike into something slicker and more modern. It just looked faster than what had come before. Cinelli’s Laser looked like a glimpse into the future back in 1981, thanks to its steel frame with ‘aero’ shapes and smoothed joints. Look at today’s 3D-printed titanium framesets and you can see the influence from this handcrafted design. Cinelli's modern reissue of its classic Laser was a limited edition back in 2012. James Huang/BikeRadar.com When Cervélo started bringing true aerodynamics to road bikes and pushed the boundaries of weight on its R series bikes, it changed the industry. It created twin arms races around aerodynamics and weight, which continue to this day. Outside of traditional performance bikes, I think of Moulton’s 1960s small-wheeled revolution and the compact, folding Brompton. And then Tern made the cargo bike an invaluable (and fashionable) accessory for parents on the school run. The Moulton Esprit retains the Moulton innovation of fast, small-wheeled bikes. Paul Smith While many of the best road bikes and best gravel bikes appear to be ‘cookie cutter’ designs, there are some signs of innovation in the world of drop-bar bikes. The rise of gravel bikes with 32in wheels is one example. The small-batch custom maker Singular jumped in and proved the divisive wheel size works , and there are plenty more 32in bikes on the way. 32in gravel bikes are an innovation championed by small builders such as Singular. Scott Windsor / ourmedia Then there’s new progressive geometry as found on the sublime Merckx 525R , which won our 2026 Race Bike of the Year award. Colnago’s impressively successful Y1Rs is welcomingly different – although it helps that it's ridden by the best rider of the current generation, Tadej Pogačar. Again, Cervélo deserves credit for bikes such as the S5 . Factor does, too, because the One looks like nothing else, and has a progressive approach to geometry to boot. Polish gravel Riding the Rondo Ruut on Polish gravel in 2017. straronphoto This brings me back to Rondo. I got to travel out to the company’s HQ in Poland back in 2017 to try out the original Ruut . It was a progressive gravel design before such a thing existed, with adjustable fork trail thanks to its flip-chip dropout – a feature now often copied across gravel bikes. The frame design looked like nothing we'd seen before, and I was sold after riding the bike on some wonderful Polish gravel trails and roads. Perhaps Rondo’s outlier status meant it approached things differently (and from what founder Szymon Koblinski has hinted to me recently, that's something it’ll continue to do). The HVRT, from 2019, is another example of this. It was three bikes in one: an aggressive aero bike; aero-endurance bike; and a 650b-wheel aero-gravel racer, before anyone else had thought about the concept of aero gravel. Then we had radical-looking bikes such as the gravity-oriented MYLC , the RATT and the last iteration of the RUUT, with its parallelogram-like back end, which combined futuristic looks and engineering to make for a more compliant rear end. I wish Rondo every success in its resurrection, and I hope more brands embrace bold design as it has. State media in Iran has reported that Iran’s delegation to the UN General Assembly had no talks planned with the United States, after US president Donald Trump said he expected more negotiations. “Iran’s delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States,” said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group. Trump told media outlet Axios on Sunday that he expected talks to resume soon, a day after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the strait of Hormuz within seven days. “Iran’s views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side... via a Qatari mediator,” IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday. Iran says it presented seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which roughly 20% of the world’s oil and gas flowed before the war. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz moved to reassure allies in Europe and Kyiv that his domestic political weakness would not erode his government’s support for Ukraine as the war nears its fifth winter. The chancellor also sought to convince an increasingly wavering German electorate that it is in their direct interest for Berlin to provide military support for Ukraine — warning that failure to remain united behind Kyiv could one day invite a Russian military attack on Germany. “If we fail to rein in Moscow, the Russian war machine will, sooner or later, turn against us and against NATO,” Merz said during a speech at a ceremony in the western German city of Münster, where the alliance was awarded the Westphalian Peace Prize. “We must not turn a blind eye to this danger. Three generations after 1945, war would return to our part of Europe.” Advertisement Advertisement Merz went on to warn of the danger of conflict in Europe with some of his most dramatic language yet. “Would the Baltic states then become a battlefield for drone warfare, just as Donbas is today?” he said. “Which major European cities would be targeted by the ballistic missiles that Russia is currently firing at the populations of Kyiv and Kharkiv?" “Would we Germans ultimately be targeted as well? Would we once again experience the horrors of war firsthand? Ladies and gentlemen, our most urgent European and transatlantic responsibility today is to do everything in our power to avert this.” Merz’s comments came weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany party recorded its best-ever election results, coming in first in two regional votes in the former East Germany, while the chancellor’s conservative Christian Democratic Union suffered historic defeats . The conservatives’ poor results were widely blamed on the deeply unpopular chancellor, prompting internal debate within his own party over whether to replace him . The surge in popularity for the Kremlin-friendly AfD sparked concerns in Kyiv and across Europe that Germany — which under Merz has become Ukraine’s greatest military supporter — could falter in its support for Ukraine. The AfD — a party that favors ending military support for Ukraine and re-establishing economic and energy ties with Moscow — is the most popular party in the country, according to surveys, polling well above Merz’s conservatives . Merz on Thursday took aim at the AfD, portraying the party as a conduit for Moscow’s influence and vowing that his government would continue to support Ukraine despite hybrid attacks and disinformation campaigns “orchestrated from Moscow” and spread through “the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers.” Advertisement Advertisement At the event in Münster, Hendrik Wüst — the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia and the conservative politician often held up as a possible replacement for Merz — praised the chancellor’s leadership in what appeared to be an effort to project unity and quell talk of a so-called “ chancellor swap .” “Chancellor Friedrich Merz assumed a pivotal role in NATO during a critical phase,” Wüst said ahead of Merz’s speech, commending the chancellor's “clear commitment” to NATO’s 5% defense spending target. “While others hesitated, the German chancellor stayed the course, thereby providing stability to the alliance,” he went on, adding: “Thanks to you, dear Friedrich, it is clear that Germany is making a strong contribution to peace and freedom.” While Merz and Wüst sought to project stability and resolve to an international audience, many of the chancellor’s remarks aimed to convince an increasingly wavering German electorate to stay the course on military support for Ukraine. Many Germans continue to express worry about a potential Russian attack on NATO territory. According to a recent survey for German public television , 42% of respondents said military support for Ukraine goes too far — the highest proportion yet. Opposition to military support for Ukraine is particularly prevalent in the former East Germany, where the AfD is strongest. “Ukraine must get through this winter, and I am convinced it will. It can count on our help,” Merz said. “If we falter in Germany, then Europe falters,” he added. “If we remain steadfast, then Europe will remain steadfast.” Advertisement Advertisement
